content.title: How to read a hemp product lab report (and why it matters more than ever in 2026)
content.excerpt: A buyer’s guide to Certificates of Analysis: what a supplier’s COA shows, how to check one in about five minutes, and what the 2026 federal hemp changes mean for the numbers on it.
content.author: Smoke Signals

body.text: Every hemp product you buy for resale should arrive with a small, unglamorous document called a Certificate of Analysis, or COA. Plenty of buyers file it without reading it. That’s a mistake — especially right now.

Federal rules for hemp products are changing in the next few weeks, and the COA is the single best tool you have to know what’s actually inside the products you source and stock. This guide walks through what a COA is, how to check one in about five minutes, and what the upcoming federal changes mean for the numbers you’ll see.

This article is written for licensed businesses and trade buyers. It is for general education only and is not legal or medical advice. Hemp-derived products are intended for adults 21 and over, and state laws vary.
Why labels alone aren’t enough
It’s easy to assume the number on the front of a supplier’s package is accurate. Independent testing says otherwise.

When the FDA tested CBD products, 18% of the 102 that listed a specific CBD amount contained significantly less than advertised and 37% contained significantly more, and 49% of the 147 products tested for cannabinoids contained some THC. A Johns Hopkins-led study of 105 topical CBD products found that only 24% of those listing a CBD amount were accurately labeled, and four products labeled “THC free” contained THC.

Potency isn’t the only concern. A study of 202 CBD products — tinctures, gummies, vapes, and topicals — found that 74% deviated from their label claim by at least 10%, and heavy metals turned up 52 times across 44 products, with lead the most common.
The takeaway isn’t that every product is bad. It’s that a trustworthy supplier can show its work, and the COA is how it does that.
What a COA is

A COA is a report from a testing laboratory showing results for a specific batch of product. According to ACS Laboratory, you can usually find it by scanning the QR code on the label or visiting the brand’s website. When you buy wholesale, ask the supplier to send the COA for each batch with the order.
A good COA covers two broad areas:

items: Potency (cannabinoid profile): How much CBD, THC, and other cannabinoids the product contains.
Safety (contaminant panels): Whether the product picked up anything harmful during growing, extraction, or manufacturing.

body.text: A potency-only report is not a full picture. As ACS Laboratory notes, a COA may report cannabinoid potency without testing for contaminants such as pesticides, heavy metals, or microbials.
How to read a COA in five minutes
Step 1: Match the batch number

Find the batch or lot number on the product or its case — often printed on the bottom of the box, the side of a bottle, or the cartridge packaging. Then confirm it matches the batch number on the COA. A report for a different batch tells you nothing about the product you received. ACS Laboratory lists this as one of the core verification steps.
Also check that the product description on the report (gummy, vape oil, tincture) matches what you ordered.
Step 2: Check the date
A COA should be recent and tied to the current batch. A general rule of thumb from LegalClarity is that a report for a current batch should be less than 12 months old.
Step 3: Look at who did the testing

The report should name an independent, third-party lab — not the brand itself. Look for ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation, the international standard for testing labs. ACS Laboratory recommends finding the accreditation number on the COA and looking it up in the accrediting organization’s database to confirm it’s current. One directory you can search is the ANSI National Accreditation Board (ANAB) directory of accredited organizations.
Worth knowing: the USDA does not require hemp labs to be ISO accredited, though it strongly encourages it. So accreditation is a quality signal you have to check for yourself.
Step 4: Read the potency section

This is the table listing cannabinoids such as CBD, CBDA, delta-9 THC, THCA, CBG, and others. Results are usually shown as a percentage, in milligrams per gram (mg/g), or in milligrams per unit or serving.
A few terms to know:

items: ND (Not Detected): The amount was below what the lab’s equipment can measure. As LegalClarity points out, ND doesn’t necessarily mean zero — check the limit of quantitation (LOQ) listed on the report.
LOQ / LOD: The lowest amount the lab can reliably measure or detect.

Percent vs. milligrams: A percentage describes concentration. Milligrams per serving or per package tells you the actual amount. With the new federal rules, the milligram-per-package number is becoming the one that matters most.

body.text: Then compare the results with the label. If a gummy says 25 mg CBD per piece, the COA should land close to that.
Step 5: Understand “Total THC”

This is the number most people misread. Raw hemp contains THCA, a precursor that converts to THC when heated. Labs account for this with a standard formula set out in the USDA’s hemp regulations and used by state regulators such as Connecticut:
Total THC = (THCA × 0.877) + delta-9 THC
The 0.877 factor comes from chemistry: when THCA converts to THC it loses a carbon dioxide group, so one gram of THCA can only become about 0.877 grams of THC.
Quick example: A COA shows 20% THCA and 0.2% delta-9 THC. (20 × 0.877) + 0.2 = 17.74% total THC.
That product might be described as having “less than 0.3% delta-9 THC,” but its total THC is far higher. If you only look at the delta-9 line, you’ll miss the full picture.
Step 6: Review the safety panels
A complete COA typically includes five contaminant panels. ACS Laboratory lists them as:

items: Pesticides: Chemical residues from farming.
Heavy metals: Lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury.
Residual solvents: Leftover chemicals from extraction.
Microbials: Bacteria, yeast, and mold.
Mycotoxins: Toxins produced by certain molds.

body.text: Each panel should show a pass or fail against a set limit — and every one should pass. If a panel is missing entirely, the report doesn’t show that the product was tested for it, so ask the supplier for the full panel.

For vape products, heavy metals deserve special attention. Metals can enter a product not only from the plant but also from the hardware. A 2021 peer-reviewed study of commercial cannabis cartridges found that metals, including small amounts of lead, migrated from the cartridge hardware into the oil and vapor. Quality cartridges and careful hardware sourcing matter, and a heavy-metals panel on the finished, filled product is the way to confirm it.
Step 7: Verify the report is real
Unfortunately, COAs can be edited. A few checks:

items: The QR code should ideally lead to the report on the lab’s own website, not just a page on the brand’s site (LegalClarity).
Watch for mismatched fonts, misaligned columns, or signs of editing.
Do the math. If the report lists CBDA and CBD, the “Total CBD” figure should equal (CBDA × 0.877) + CBD — the same formula used for THC.
When in doubt, contact the lab directly with the batch number.

body.text: One more reason to look closely: a study of 97 CBD haircare, cosmetic, and food and drink products found that label accuracy did not differ significantly between products that claimed third-party testing and those that didn’t. A “lab tested” badge isn’t the same as a lab report you’ve actually read.
What the 2026 federal hemp changes mean for buyers

In November 2025, Congress changed the federal definition of hemp as part of a spending bill (Public Law 119-37). The changes were originally set to take effect November 12, 2026, but a later funding bill (Public Law 119-103) delayed most of them to December 11, 2026.
Here’s the current timeline, based on the two laws, the Congressional Research Service, and legal analysis from Fox Rothschild:

items: November 12, 2026: Products containing cannabinoids that are “not capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant” no longer meet the federal definition of hemp.

December 11, 2026: Most other changes take effect. They include a total THC standard (counting THCA), the exclusion of cannabinoids synthesized or manufactured outside the plant, and a cap of 0.4 milligrams combined total per container of total THC and other cannabinoids with similar effects in finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products.

body.text: Federal law defines “container” as the innermost wrapping, packaging, or vessel in direct contact with the final product, in which it is enclosed for retail sale. The law directs the FDA to publish further detail, which it had not done as of October 28, 2026. Legal commentators describe slightly different groupings for lab-converted cannabinoids such as delta-8, so check current guidance for specific products.

To put 0.4 mg in perspective: a single hemp gummy with 5 mg of delta-9 THC would exceed the cap more than twelve times over in one piece. Leafwell notes that most delta-8 products, hemp delta-9 gummies, and THC drinks would fall above the limit once the change takes effect.

The date could still move. December 11 is also the next federal funding deadline. Bills to delay or repeal the new definition have been introduced, but as of October 28, 2026, none had advanced past committee, according to the Congressional Research Service and DPS Law. Some states also set their own, stricter rules — Minnesota’s Office of Cannabis Management, for example, has published guidance on how the federal change affects products there.
What this means for reading COAs:

items: Look for total THC, not just delta-9 THC. Under the new definition, THCA counts.
Look for milligrams per package, not just percentages. A low percentage can still add up to more than 0.4 mg across a full container.
Expect labels and product lines to change. Brands may reformulate, and older inventory may not reflect current rules. A current, batch-matched COA is your best way to know what you’re buying.

body.text: A quick buyer’s checklist
Before you place or accept an order, confirm:

items: The product has a QR code or a clear link to its COA.
The batch number on the package matches the COA.
The report is recent (generally under 12 months).
An independent, ISO/IEC 17025-accredited lab did the testing.
Cannabinoid results match the label within a reasonable range.
Total THC is listed (or you can calculate it).
All five safety panels are present and passing.
The report links back to the lab’s own site, or you can verify it with the lab.

body.text: If a supplier can’t or won’t provide a COA, that tells you something too.
The bottom line

A COA turns a product from a promise into something you can check. With federal definitions shifting on November 12 and December 11, the details on that report — total THC, milligrams per package, and complete safety testing — matter more than ever.
Whoever you source from, ask for the lab report with every batch and take five minutes to read it. Good suppliers are glad you asked.
